aldemar.headline: Friday's AI scare lasted one session — and then a protest in Paris moved US Treasuries
aldemar.standfirst: Tech and AI shares led a rebound from the previous week's heavy losses: the Nasdaq rose 1.11% and the S&P 0.41%, while most shares outside AI and technology fell and the Dow slipped 0.07% — the fourth different leader in four sessions. The yields moved for a reason that had nothing to do with America: violent weekend protests across France over the cost of living and school conditions brought more than 2,000 arrests, with clashes in Milan too, and Prime Minister Lecornu did not rule out a state of emergency. France's ten-year rose 13 basis points to 4.93%, the sharpest in the G7; the CAC fell 1.5% and Italy and Spain 1.9% each; the euro hit a 17-month low against the pound. US Treasuries followed on no American data, the ten-year +4bp to about 5.13% and the thirty-year to 5.47%. And Gulf crude flows more than halved, to a seven-day average of about 8.5m barrels a day from over 20m, after a tanker hit a naval mine in Hormuz and the Houthis claimed strikes on Yanbu, Shaybah and the airports at Riyadh and Abha; WTI settled $103.66, its highest since 15 September. In the book AMZN rose 4.98% to 262.45 — two cents from where it closed on 9 October — and PLTR 4.36%, while AAPL fell 0.15% and was the only faller. A net of +47.62. Heat 3.00R against 3.0R, unchanged for a twenty-eighth session. The foldable reaches shops on Friday.

Conviction that reverses every day is not conviction.

2. French domestic politics set the price of American debt, and that is the global-debt thesis arriving in a form you can see. Weekend protests over the cost of living and school conditions produced more than 2,000 arrests and clashes in Milan; Lecornu asked for curfews and would not rule out a state of emergency. France's ten-year rose 13 basis points to 4.93%, the sharpest move in the G7, and yields rose across Europe and then in the United States — ten-year +4bp to about 5.13%, thirty-year +4bp to 5.47% — on no American data. The reason this matters beyond a day's move: France's deficit is heading for 5.4% of GDP and its 2027 austerity budget faces a parliamentary vote next month. The arithmetic requires spending cuts; the street has just rejected them. A term premium is the price of exactly that gap, and this is the first time it has been visible rather than inferred.

3. Gulf crude flows more than halved in a week, and that is the largest supply fact of the whole conflict. The seven-day average fell to about 8.5m barrels a day from over 20m the previous week, after at least ten incidents involving commercial vessels; Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a tanker exploded after hitting a naval mine in the southern Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. The Houthis claimed strikes on an Aramco facility at Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and airports at Riyadh and Abha — unconfirmed by Saudi authorities and not independently verified — following an attack in Yemen's Shabwa province that killed 53 people. Against all of it, Trump signed an executive order waiving certain sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy exports, which analysts read as an attempt to ease fuel prices before the 3 November midterms, with implementation uncertain. WTI settled $103.66, its highest since 15 September.

Gulf flows fell from twenty million barrels a day to eight and a half

That is the number. Gulf crude flows fell to a seven-day average of about 8.5m barrels a day, down from over 20m the previous week, after at least ten incidents involving commercial vessels. On Sunday Iran's Revolutionary Guards said an oil tanker exploded after hitting a naval mine in the southern Strait of Hormuz. A fortnight ago this brief was reporting Gulf exports at 13.9m barrels a day, over 75% of pre-war levels, and Kpler warning that the recovery would be uneven. It has not been uneven; it has reversed.

And the targets widened again. The Houthis claimed strikes on an Aramco facility at Yanbu — the Red Sea terminal whose purpose is to bypass Hormuz, and the same port a Saudi-led coalition intercepted a ballistic missile over on Friday — along with the Shaybah oilfield and airports at Riyadh and Abha. Saudi authorities have not confirmed any of it and none of it has been independently verified, so it is a claim rather than a fact. It followed an attack in Yemen's Shabwa province that killed 53 people. Whether or not the strikes landed, a campaign that now names the capital's airport and the hedge against the chokepoint is a different campaign from the one that was attacking tankers three weeks ago.

The offset is political and explicitly dated. Trump signed an executive order waiving certain sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy exports. Analysts read it as an attempt to ease fuel prices before the 3 November midterms; implementation is uncertain. It is the mirror image of the IEA and reserve releases that failed to hold the price down on Friday — a supply-side intervention aimed at the pump rather than at the barrel — and it is the clearest statement yet of how much the energy line in the inflation data now matters politically. Brent took it as a reason to sell: $109.55, down 31 cents, on profit-taking after a five-month high.

WTI went the other way, and the spread is the thing to watch now. WTI settled $103.66, up $2.25 or 2.2%, its highest settlement since 15 September, so the gap to Brent collapsed to $5.89 from $8.45 — and from $12.91 a week ago. The American barrel is tightening against the world's at speed, which is a function of the 8.6m-barrel US inventory draw reported on Friday rather than of anything in the Gulf. For this book the transmission is unchanged and getting stronger: gasoline did over half of September's CPI increase, crude has gone from $90.76 to $103.66 in six sessions, and the October print lands 10 November.

September CPI came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year and September PPI at +1.3% against +0.5% expected — yet the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%, with hike odds for 28 October ending near 27% after touching 50%. A week in which the small-cap index has its most unusual move of the series, the Nasdaq has its worst week since June, crude rises eleven percent and gold does not move at all is not a week with one story in it.

The indices, precisely. Across the five sessions the S&P fell 152.10 points, or 1.9%, to 7,659.44; the Nasdaq 1,226.14, or 4.5%, to 26,140.03 — its worst week since June, as was the S&P's; the Russell 85.61, or 3%, to 2,721.37. The Dow rose 347.46 points, or 0.7%, to 52,002.41, and was the only index up. For the year the S&P is now up 11.9%, the Nasdaq 12.5%, the Russell 9.6% and the Dow 8.2% — the Dow has closed almost the whole of the gap the Nasdaq built over the first nine months.

Two first-tier prints, both hot, and the long end fell anyway. September CPI on Wednesday came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year, core +0.3% and +2.6%, both above forecast — with gasoline +9.1% and +34.2% doing over half the monthly increase on the BLS's own reckoning, and shelter and core services both accelerating to +0.4%. September PPI on Thursday came in at +1.3% against +0.5% expected, +6.3% on the year, with energy goods +10.8% and gasoline +20.3% at the producer level. Hike odds for 28 October went from about 22% to roughly 50% to about 27% inside three sessions. And the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year about 17, at 5.43%. Fed Chair Warsh's IMF remarks left roughly an 85% hold priced for this month.

The number that explains it is in the retail sales report, not the inflation ones. Headline retail sales rose 0.8% against 0.3% expected, to $745.0bn. But the control group rose only 0.1% against 0.3% expected, and excluding petrol stations the increase was 0.2%. So the consumer is not spending more; the consumer is paying more for fuel. Gasoline did over half of CPI, rose a fifth at the producer level, and supplied most of the retail beat. The bond market read that as a tax on demand rather than inflation to be met with hikes, and bought duration into two hot prints. That is the single most important thing the week established.

And crude broke a hundred dollars. WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41, +11.7%, and Brent from $103.35 to $109.86, touching $110 on Friday for the first time since May. Gold finished the week almost exactly where it started, at $4,166.39, having fallen 1.34% on the CPI and risen 1.60% on the PPI. Where the quarter stands · twelve sessions in

Q4 is +131.02 at +6.55R, of which none is realised: it is open profit accrued since entry, not a Q4 return. Q3 finished at +17.04, +0.84R, against the S&P's +2.0%. On $1,335.73 of capital still committed the open book is +9.81% since entry. The week cost -98.36 against an S&P down 1.9%, a Nasdaq down 4.5% and a Dow up 0.7%, which is the comparison that matters: 2 of the 4 positions are above +1R (AAPL at +1.08R, AMZN at +5.17R), and the index this book owns nothing in was the only one that rose.

Two hot prints, a bank fine, a foldable sell-out, and a rotation that completed

1. The long end fell through two hot inflation prints, and that settles a three-week argument. The thesis built from 29 September was that the long end was rising on supply and global debt rather than inflation. This week tested it to destruction: the ten-year spiked to 5.33% on the CPI and closed back at 5.19%; then fell 12 basis points on the PPI to a three-week low; and finished the week about 14 basis points lower, with the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%. Neither explanation survives. An inflation trade would have risen and stayed risen. A pure supply trade would not have spiked on CPI at all. What fits is the retail sales control group at +0.1%: the market read energy-driven price rises as demand destruction and bought duration into them. Hike odds for 28 October ended the week near 27% after touching 50%.

2. The banks reported and the split told you where the cycle is. JPMorgan missed for the first time in nearly three years — $5.57 against $5.93 expected — on investment banking and a fixed-income desk that slowed from the summer. Goldman earned $17.01 against $12.25 a year ago on stock trading, with bond trading slower. Citigroup's profit rose 40% but card profits were flat. Bank of America missed on Wednesday — $0.91 a share including a charge, $1.08 against $1.10 excluding it, revenue $30bn against $30.58bn, investment banking fees −11% and sales and trading −5% — the day after the Treasury fined it $1.2bn, the third-largest penalty in that department's history, for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations involving more than $5bn of suspicious transactions. The pattern: equity desks busy, bond desks quiet, consumer flat.

3. Apple's foldable sold out in minutes, which was the only checkable fact in a fortnight of sourcing. Three parties had disagreed from anonymous supply-chain contacts — Nikkei on iPhone 18 Pro cuts, Securities Times on Duo orders raised 30% toward ten million units, Bank of America on shorter Pro delivery times — and Friday replaced all of it with evidence. Pre-orders opened at 8am Eastern, stock went within moments, shipping slipped to late January 2027 on some configurations, Apple called demand nothing short of extraordinary, and units resold at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list. The fair caveat is that a sell-out is a ratio and Apple probably built few of them. The resale premium is harder to argue with.

4. And the rotation completed, which is the week's real lesson for this book. Over five sessions the Dow rose 0.7% and was the only index up, while the Nasdaq fell 4.5% and the Russell 3%. Friday's sell-off is the one to study: the Nasdaq fell 2.15% and the Dow 0.34% while the ten-year rose two basis points. That was not a rate event. Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% as investors grew more concerned about how long AI infrastructure spending will last, and Okta, Palantir, Datadog, Zscaler and Elastic were sold together. A rate scare reverses when the Fed is repriced — and it did, on Thursday. A thesis under question does not.

Crude rose eleven percent through two emergency releases

WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41 across the week, up 11.7%, and Brent touched $110 on Friday for the first time since May. It did so through four separate supply events and against the two largest tools short of policy that the agencies have. Monday: +3.28% on renewed Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Tuesday: WTI up, Brent down, as traders weighed a possible US–Russia diesel deal against escalation in Yemen. Wednesday: +1.01% after a Houthi missile hit an office tower at Aramco's Dhahran headquarters — top three floors damaged, limited fire, no injuries, a command centre rather than a producing asset. Thursday: +3.03% on a US inventory draw. Friday: +3.51%.

Friday's reasons are worth separating because one of them is new. A Saudi-led coalition intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu — the Red Sea export terminal whose entire strategic value is that crude leaving from it bypasses the Strait of Hormuz. Targeting the hedge against the chokepoint is an escalation in kind, not degree. Ukrainian strikes also damaged the Ryazan refinery, shutting a primary crude unit, which bears directly on Russian diesel. And the EIA reported US crude stocks down 8.6m barrels to 415.6m, with distillates down 2.5m.

Against all of which: the IEA announced the release of over 20m barrels of emergency supply, and Washington offered up to 17m through a reserve exchange. Roughly 37m barrels of announced additional supply, and the price rose 3.5% on the day and 11.7% on the week. The reason is the number Aramco's Amin Nasser has been repeating: commercial inventory under 6 billion barrels against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, with less than 10% practically available and up to two years to rebuild. A release needs a cushion to land on. There is not one.

And the diesel number is how all of this reaches a book with no oil position in it. The IEA reported combined net gasoil exports from the Middle East and Russia down 1.3m barrels a day in September to 820,000 — more than 60% lower year on year — with no stock rebuild expected before the second half of 2027, because the binding constraint is how much Russian refining capacity is actually running. Gulf crude exports are back at 13.9m barrels a day, over 75% of pre-war; refined product exports are 1.9m against 4.7m. Crude flows and product does not. That gap is why gasoline rose 20.3% at the producer level in September and did over half of the CPI increase — and the October print, due 10 November, carries a crude price eleven percent higher than when this week began.

The Nasdaq fell 4.48% at 1.99σ, crude rose 11.73% at 1.85σ and the S&P fell 1.95% at 1.69σ. And then the two that did nothing: the Dow rose 0.67% at 0.63σ and gold fell 0.20% at 0.13σ. A week in which the small-cap index has its most unusual move of the series, the Nasdaq has its worst week since June, crude rises eleven percent and gold does not move at all is not a week with one story in it.

The indices, precisely. Across the five sessions the S&P fell 152.10 points, or 1.9%, to 7,659.44; the Nasdaq 1,226.14, or 4.5%, to 26,140.03 — its worst week since June, as was the S&P's; the Russell 85.61, or 3%, to 2,721.37. The Dow rose 347.46 points, or 0.7%, to 52,002.41, and was the only index up. For the year the S&P is now up 11.9%, the Nasdaq 12.5%, the Russell 9.6% and the Dow 8.2% — the Dow has closed almost the whole of the gap the Nasdaq built over the first nine months.

Two first-tier prints, both hot, and the long end fell anyway. September CPI on Wednesday came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year, core +0.3% and +2.6%, both above forecast — with gasoline +9.1% and +34.2% doing over half the monthly increase on the BLS's own reckoning, and shelter and core services both accelerating to +0.4%. September PPI on Thursday came in at +1.3% against +0.5% expected, +6.3% on the year, with energy goods +10.8% and gasoline +20.3% at the producer level. Hike odds for 28 October went from about 22% to roughly 50% to about 27% inside three sessions. And the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year about 17, at 5.43%. Fed Chair Warsh's IMF remarks left roughly an 85% hold priced for this month.

The number that explains it is in the retail sales report, not the inflation ones. Headline retail sales rose 0.8% against 0.3% expected, to $745.0bn. But the control group rose only 0.1% against 0.3% expected, and excluding petrol stations the increase was 0.2%. So the consumer is not spending more; the consumer is paying more for fuel. Gasoline did over half of CPI, rose a fifth at the producer level, and supplied most of the retail beat. The bond market read that as a tax on demand rather than inflation to be met with hikes, and bought duration into two hot prints. That is the single most important thing the week established.

And crude broke a hundred dollars. WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41, +11.7%, and Brent from $103.35 to $109.86, touching $110 on Friday for the first time since May. Gold finished the week almost exactly where it started, at $4,166.39, having fallen 1.34% on the CPI and risen 1.60% on the PPI. An eleven-percent week in oil and a flat week in gold is a market pricing a supply problem, not a monetary one.

The worst week of the stretch — and the R column is the part to read

GOOGInternet content · entered 2026-07-27 at 325.86 · stop 305.67 · 9.27% away · managed+0.55R-3.15%-10.95
AAPLConsumer electronics · entered 2026-08-28 at 321.97 · stop 301.26 · 12.29% away+1.04R+2.03%+6.82
OKTASoftware: identity & security · entered 2026-09-14 at 182.73 · stop 162.61 · 13.16% away+0.23R-19.33%-44.87
AMZNInternet retail · entered 2026-10-06 at 251.84 · closed 2026-10-15 at 250.89 · gapped through the 251.84 stop-0.14R-4.40%-34.62

The percentage and dollar columns above are the week, 12 to 16 October. The R column is where each position stands against the risk it was opened with. The book moved -83.62 across the five sessions and now shows +37.07 open at +1.81R. One position closed: AMZN was stopped out on Wednesday the 15th, gapping through its breakeven stop at the open, realising -2.85 or -0.14R — and costing -34.62 measured from the previous Friday's close. The nearest line on the week's lows was GOOG, 8.89% above its 305.67 stop. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap (2.04R excluding the managed GOOG position) and has not moved since 14 September.

OKTA is the week. It fell 19.3% across five consecutive losing sessions, from 232.13 to 187.26, taking −44.87 out of the book — more than half the week's loss on its own. On Monday it opened at 235.00, a 52-week high; by Friday it had fallen 10.20% in a single session, the largest of its life. The position has gone from +2.46R to +0.23R. There was no company news in any of the five sessions. What there was instead: a stock up 152.4% on the year, one screen calling it 102.4% above intrinsic value, $54.8m of insider selling over twelve months, and agent revenue not forecast to begin until fiscal 2028. The 5 October valuation note has now largely been settled against the position.

AAPL was the only thing that worked, and only at the end. It rose 2.0% across the week while the Nasdaq fell 4.5%, and at +1.04R it is the only position left above +1R, carrying 58% of the open profit. The week's argument about iPhone demand ran through three contradictory supply-chain reports and was then settled on Friday by the only checkable event in it: the iPhone Duo sold out within moments of pre-orders opening, Apple called the demand nothing short of extraordinary, shipping slipped to late January 2027 on some configurations, and units resold at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list. GOOG, meanwhile, fell 3.2% to +0.55R, its lowest close since 2 October.

And the AMZN exit is the week's lesson, stated once. The stop was at the fill, 251.84, which made the position riskless in the sense that mattered: no capital could be lost. It did not make the fill riskless. On Wednesday the stock gapped to a 250.89 open, ninety-five cents below the stop, with no trade in between — so the exit was the open, not the stop, and the trade realised -2.85 instead of nothing. It then fell to 248.65 and closed 254.76, above the stop. In a $250 stock that can gap three dollars overnight, a breakeven stop means risk of about a dollar a share, and the position most likely to be taken out is the one with the tightest line regardless of how safe that line looks. Heat did not fall when it closed, either — a stop at the entry was carrying no risk, so removing it freed none.

Where the quarter stands · twelve sessions in

Q4 is +34.22 at +1.67R, of which -2.85 is realised and the rest is open profit accrued since entry — not a Q4 return. Q3 finished at +12.31, +0.58R, against the S&P's +2.0%. On $830.56 of capital still committed the open book is +4.46% since entry. The week cost -83.62 against an S&P down 1.9%, a Nasdaq down 4.5% and a Dow up 0.7%, which is the comparison that matters: 1 of the 3 positions is above +1R (AAPL at +1.04R), and the index this book owns nothing in was the only one that rose.

Two hot prints, a bank fine, a foldable sell-out, and a rotation that completed

1. The long end fell through two hot inflation prints, and that settles a three-week argument. The thesis built from 29 September was that the long end was rising on supply and global debt rather than inflation. This week tested it to destruction: the ten-year spiked to 5.33% on the CPI and closed back at 5.19%; then fell 12 basis points on the PPI to a three-week low; and finished the week about 14 basis points lower, with the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%. Neither explanation survives. An inflation trade would have risen and stayed risen. A pure supply trade would not have spiked on CPI at all. What fits is the retail sales control group at +0.1%: the market read energy-driven price rises as demand destruction and bought duration into them. Hike odds for 28 October ended the week near 27% after touching 50%.

2. The banks reported and the split told you where the cycle is. JPMorgan missed for the first time in nearly three years — $5.57 against $5.93 expected — on investment banking and a fixed-income desk that slowed from the summer. Goldman earned $17.01 against $12.25 a year ago on stock trading, with bond trading slower. Citigroup's profit rose 40% but card profits were flat. Bank of America missed on Wednesday — $0.91 a share including a charge, $1.08 against $1.10 excluding it, revenue $30bn against $30.58bn, investment banking fees −11% and sales and trading −5% — the day after the Treasury fined it $1.2bn, the third-largest penalty in that department's history, for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations involving more than $5bn of suspicious transactions. The pattern: equity desks busy, bond desks quiet, consumer flat.

3. Apple's foldable sold out in minutes, which was the only checkable fact in a fortnight of sourcing. Three parties had disagreed from anonymous supply-chain contacts — Nikkei on iPhone 18 Pro cuts, Securities Times on Duo orders raised 30% toward ten million units, Bank of America on shorter Pro delivery times — and Friday replaced all of it with evidence. Pre-orders opened at 8am Eastern, stock went within moments, shipping slipped to late January 2027 on some configurations, Apple called demand nothing short of extraordinary, and units resold at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list. The fair caveat is that a sell-out is a ratio and Apple probably built few of them. The resale premium is harder to argue with.

4. And the rotation completed, which is the week's real lesson for this book. Over five sessions the Dow rose 0.7% and was the only index up, while the Nasdaq fell 4.5% and the Russell 3%. Friday's sell-off is the one to study: the Nasdaq fell 2.15% and the Dow 0.34% while the ten-year rose two basis points. That was not a rate event. Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% as investors grew more concerned about how long AI infrastructure spending will last, and Okta, Palantir, Datadog, Zscaler and Elastic were sold together. A rate scare reverses when the Fed is repriced — and it did, on Thursday. A thesis under question does not.

Crude rose eleven percent through two emergency releases

WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41 across the week, up 11.7%, and Brent touched $110 on Friday for the first time since May. It did so through four separate supply events and against the two largest tools short of policy that the agencies have. Monday: +3.28% on renewed Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Tuesday: WTI up, Brent down, as traders weighed a possible US–Russia diesel deal against escalation in Yemen. Wednesday: +1.01% after a Houthi missile hit an office tower at Aramco's Dhahran headquarters — top three floors damaged, limited fire, no injuries, a command centre rather than a producing asset. Thursday: +3.03% on a US inventory draw. Friday: +3.51%.

Friday's reasons are worth separating because one of them is new. A Saudi-led coalition intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu — the Red Sea export terminal whose entire strategic value is that crude leaving from it bypasses the Strait of Hormuz. Targeting the hedge against the chokepoint is an escalation in kind, not degree. Ukrainian strikes also damaged the Ryazan refinery, shutting a primary crude unit, which bears directly on Russian diesel. And the EIA reported US crude stocks down 8.6m barrels to 415.6m, with distillates down 2.5m.

Against all of which: the IEA announced the release of over 20m barrels of emergency supply, and Washington offered up to 17m through a reserve exchange. Roughly 37m barrels of announced additional supply, and the price rose 3.5% on the day and 11.7% on the week. The reason is the number Aramco's Amin Nasser has been repeating: commercial inventory under 6 billion barrels against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, with less than 10% practically available and up to two years to rebuild. A release needs a cushion to land on. There is not one.

And the diesel number is how all of this reaches a book with no oil position in it. The IEA reported combined net gasoil exports from the Middle East and Russia down 1.3m barrels a day in September to 820,000 — more than 60% lower year on year — with no stock rebuild expected before the second half of 2027, because the binding constraint is how much Russian refining capacity is actually running. Gulf crude exports are back at 13.9m barrels a day, over 75% of pre-war; refined product exports are 1.9m against 4.7m. Crude flows and product does not. That gap is why gasoline rose 20.3% at the producer level in September and did over half of the CPI increase — and the October print, due 10 November, carries a crude price eleven percent higher than when this week began.

Ten days of empty calendar, then four events in three days

There is nothing dated for ten days, and that has not been true since late September. No print, no earnings, no scheduled event from any company held, until the Duo ships on Friday 23 October. Then the calendar compresses: the Fed and Alphabet on Wednesday the 28th, Apple and Amazon on Thursday the 29th, Palantir on 2 November and October CPI on the 10th. Four of the five positions this book has held during October report inside those three days.

Alphabet on the 28th is the one that has changed character. A fortnight ago its $195-205bn of capex and the 3.6-gigawatt Constellation deal were the bull case — evidence of scale. After a Friday in which Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% because investors are no longer sure how long AI infrastructure spending lasts, the same number is the thing the print has to defend. And it lands the same afternoon the Fed decides, so two factors resolve on one day for a book exposed to both.

What to watch in this book. Whether AAPL holds what the pre-order gave it — at +1.04R it is the only position above +1R and carries 58% of the open profit, a concentration that arrived by subtraction. Whether OKTA finds a floor at +0.23R after nineteen percent in five sessions. And whether GOOG can hold 335 into its own print. All of them now turn on one question, and it is no longer the Fed: whether the market still believes the AI build.

The standing position: do nothing, because nothing can be done. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap and has not moved in twenty-seven sessions, so no position can be added however attractive anything looks. This week was the first real test of that constraint: two holdings fell more than ten percent, one closed, and the book could not respond to any of it. The ten days to the 23rd are the first stretch since September with nothing to react to, which makes them the right time to decide what this book should look like when it can act again.
